walkthroughs.title: Adding a computed column and keeping a schema when no rows match

steps.excerpt:
"""polars-001: complete bounded Polars investigation."""

import polars as pl
steps.title: Import Polars
steps.explanation: Polars is a DataFrame library built around expressions: you describe a column computation with pl.col and Polars evaluates it, often in parallel. The pl alias is the common convention.
steps.observe: Only Polars is imported. The data is written inline, so the program reads no files.

steps.title: Build a frame and derive revenue
steps.explanation: pl.DataFrame takes a dictionary of column name to values. with_columns returns a new frame with extra or replaced columns; it does not change frame in place. The expression pl.col("units") * pl.col("price") multiplies row by row, and alias names the result revenue.
steps.observe: result has four columns: the three originals plus revenue.

steps.excerpt:
assert frame.shape == (3, 3) and result.shape == (3, 4)
    assert result["revenue"].to_list() == [10, 8, 12]
    assert result.select(pl.col("revenue").sum()).item() == 30
    assert "revenue" not in frame.columns
    return {"rows": result.to_dicts(), "total_revenue": 30}
steps.title: Check shapes, values and immutability
steps.explanation: shape is (rows, columns). The revenue values are 2 times 5, 1 times 8 and 4 times 3. select(pl.col("revenue").sum()) builds a one cell frame and item() pulls the scalar out. The last assert proves the original frame was not modified, which is how Polars avoids hidden side effects.
steps.observe: The returned dictionary holds the rows as a list of dicts and total_revenue 30.

steps.title: Declare a schema and filter to nothing
steps.explanation: Passing schema= fixes each column's data type instead of letting Polars infer it. filter keeps rows where the condition is true; no id exceeds 10, so empty has zero rows. The important check is that the empty result still has the same columns and types.
steps.observe: empty.height is 0, yet empty.schema still says id is Int64 and label is String.

steps.title: Choose column order with select
steps.explanation: select with column names returns those columns in the order given, so label now comes before id. The function returns the empty frame's shape and a text form of its schema.
steps.observe: empty_shape is (0, 2): zero rows, two columns.

steps.title: Print both results and a pass marker
steps.explanation: main prints each returned dictionary and then a final marker. Every assert has to pass before the marker line is reached.
steps.observe: The output ends with polars-001 reference checks passed.

walkthroughs.title: Time zones across a daylight saving jump and half open time windows

steps.excerpt:
from datetime import UTC, datetime

import polars as pl
steps.title: Standard datetime and Polars
steps.explanation: UTC is the standard library's UTC time zone object, and datetime builds timezone aware timestamps. Aware timestamps carry their zone, which prevents silent mixing of local and universal time.
steps.observe: Both imports are needed: datetime for literal timestamps and Polars for the frames.

steps.title: Parse UTC strings and convert to New York
steps.explanation: str.to_datetime parses ISO text into a datetime column marked as UTC. dt.convert_time_zone keeps the same instant but changes how it is displayed. On March 10, 2024 New York clocks jumped from 2:00 to 3:00, so two instants one hour apart show local hours 1 and 3.
steps.observe: local has three columns: the original text, the UTC instant and the New York display.

steps.title: Display hours differ by two, elapsed time by one
steps.explanation: dt.hour reads the local clock hour. Subtracting the two UTC values gives a duration, and total_seconds converts it to a number. The lesson: compute durations on instants, not on displayed local hours.
steps.observe: display_hours is [1, 3] while elapsed_seconds is 3600, exactly one hour.

steps.excerpt:
def example_two():
    timestamps = [
        datetime(2024, 1, 1, tzinfo=UTC),
        datetime(2024, 1, 2, tzinfo=UTC),
        datetime(2024, 1, 3, tzinfo=UTC),
    ]
    frame = pl.DataFrame({"time": timestamps, "amount": [2, 3, 5]})
    start, end = timestamps[0], timestamps[2]
    period = frame.filter((pl.col("time") >= start) & (pl.col("time") < end))
steps.title: A half open reporting window
steps.explanation: Three daily timestamps carry amounts 2, 3 and 5. The filter keeps rows with start <= time < end. Including the start and excluding the end is called half open, and it means consecutive windows never double count a boundary row. The & operator combines two column conditions; each side needs its own parentheses.
steps.observe: period contains only the first two days, whose amounts total 5.

steps.excerpt:
assert period["amount"].sum() == 5
    assert frame.filter(pl.col("time") >= end)["amount"].sum() == 5
    assert period.height + frame.filter(pl.col("time") >= end).height == frame.height
    return {"half_open_total": 5, "next_period_total": 5}
steps.title: Prove the windows partition the data
steps.explanation: The next window starts exactly at end, so the row at January 3 belongs there. The third assert checks that the two windows together contain every row exactly once.
steps.observe: half_open_total and next_period_total are both 5, and no row is lost or counted twice.

steps.title: Print results and the pass marker
steps.explanation: main prints both dictionaries and then the marker line, which appears only when all checks pass.
steps.observe: The last line is polars-007 reference checks passed.

walkthroughs.title: Point in time joins that avoid using information from the future

steps.excerpt:
def example_one():
    requests = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "time": [2, 5, 9]}).sort("time")
    features = pl.DataFrame({"time": [1, 4, 8], "value": [10, 20, 30]}).sort("time")
    past = requests.join_asof(features, on="time", strategy="backward", tolerance=2)
    future = requests.join_asof(features, on="time", strategy="forward")
steps.title: As of joins in both directions
steps.explanation: join_asof matches each request to the nearest feature row by time instead of requiring equal times. Both frames must be sorted on the key. strategy="backward" takes the latest feature at or before the request time, with tolerance=2 limiting how stale it may be. strategy="forward" takes the next feature after the request, which would leak the future into a model.
steps.observe: past and future each have one row per request, with a value column added from features.

steps.title: Compare the honest and the leaking match
steps.explanation: Backward matching gives 10, 20 and 30, each known before its request. Forward matching gives 20, 30 and then None, because the last request has no later feature. The forward result is kept only as a counterexample.
steps.observe: past_only uses values from the past. lookahead_counterexample shows what leakage looks like.

steps.title: Event time versus knowledge time
steps.explanation: Each feature row has an event time, when something happened, and a known time, when the system learned about it. The 999 value describes an event at time 4 that was not known until time 7. A request with cutoff 5 must not use it.
steps.observe: The trap row is event 4, known 7, value 999.

steps.excerpt:
candidates = requests.join(features, on="customer").filter(
        (pl.col("event") <= pl.col("cutoff")) & (pl.col("known") <= pl.col("cutoff"))
    )
    correct = (
        candidates.sort("request", "event", "known").group_by("request", maintain_order=True).last()
    )
    assert correct["value"].to_list() == [10, 30]
steps.title: Filter on both times, then take the latest
steps.explanation: Joining on customer pairs every request with every feature row. The filter keeps rows where both the event and the knowledge happened by the cutoff. Sorting and then group_by with maintain_order=True followed by last picks the most recent eligible feature per request.
steps.observe: correct gives 10 for the cutoff 5 request and 30 for the cutoff 9 request.

steps.excerpt:
leaking = (
        requests.join(features, on="customer")
        .filter(pl.col("event") <= pl.col("cutoff"))
        .sort("request", "event")
        .group_by("request", maintain_order=True)
        .last()
    )
    assert leaking["value"].to_list() == [999, 30]
    return {"available_values": [10, 30], "event_time_only_values": [999, 30]}
steps.title: The leaking version for comparison
steps.explanation: This chain filters only on event time. Method chaining inside parentheses lets each step sit on its own line. Request 1 now picks up 999, a value the system did not know at cutoff 5.
steps.observe: event_time_only_values is [999, 30]; the first value is a leak.

steps.title: Print results and the pass marker
steps.explanation: main prints both dictionaries and then the marker line after every check succeeds.
steps.observe: The last line is polars-014 reference checks passed.
